title: Grouped fractions and weighted totals
transcript: Grouped fractions refer to different group sizes. Find the actual contribution from each group before combining them. A combined proportion is the total success count divided by the total group size.

In AMC practice, a problem may give fractions for two groups of people or objects. Convert each fraction into a count. A Rossmoyne style problem can work in reverse: use the combined total to recover the size of one group.
One third of eighteen red cards and one quarter of twenty-four blue cards are starred. How many starred cards are there? Find both counts separately, then add them.
One third of eighteen is six. One quarter of twenty-four is six. These are different cards, so their counts add. There are twelve starred cards.

The same groups have forty-two cards in total. One third of the red group of eighteen and one quarter of the blue group of twenty-four are starred. What fraction of all the cards are starred? Identify the numerator and denominator separately.

The numerator is the count of starred cards. The two contributions are six and six, or twelve in total. The full collection has forty-two cards. Put the starred count over that full size. In lowest terms that is two over seven. This uses actual counts, so the unequal group sizes have their proper weight.

There are eighty-four items in groups A and B. Half of A and one third of B are marked. In total thirty-three items are marked. Find the size of each group. Compare the actual marked count with what one third of the entire collection would give.

If every item used the lower rate, one third of eighty-four would give twenty-eight marks. The extra is five marks. Every item in A adds a difference of one half minus one third, which is one sixth of a mark. Six times the excess gives group A's size, thirty. Subtract that from the full size to find group B, fifty-four.
Check the actual marked count. Half of A gives fifteen. One third of B gives eighteen. Both the total size and the marked count match. The fixed difference in rates determines A uniquely.

Adding the fractions of two separate groups does not add their amounts. Multiply by each corresponding group size first. For the combined proportion, use the combined size, including unmarked items and every group.

Write one row per group with its size, rate and contribution. Keep those three columns distinct. When the combined amount is known, compare with a simple baseline. Test the recovered group sizes with both original totals.
